headline: A T. rex skeleton sells for 50 million dollars

sources.title: Mystery bidder buys T. rex nicknamed 'Gus' for a record $50 million
T. rex sells for $50 million, becoming the most expensive dinosaur fossil ever auctioned
Rare T. rex fossil sells for record $50.1 million at auction

chunks.text: A skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex sold for 50.1 million dollars in New York on July 14. The [[auction house]] had expected it to {{go for}} 20 to 30 million, so the price almost doubled the highest [[estimate]]. The buyer [[bid]] by telephone and has not been named. No dinosaur has ever sold for more. The old [[record]] was almost 45 million dollars, paid for a stegosaurus in 2024. The sale has {{stirred up}} an old argument about who should be allowed to own a [[fossil]] like this.

verbs.correct: To be sold for a price
verbs.wrong: To be valued before the sale
To bring an old argument to an end

chunks.text: The skeleton is [[nicknamed]] Gus. It is about 67 million years old, 38 feet long and 12.5 feet tall. A team {{dug up}} the bones on a [[ranch]] in South Dakota in 2021. Freeing them from the rock and then {{cleaning up}} every piece took five years. The ranch belonged to a farmer called Gary Licking, and he died before that work was finished. The team chose the nickname in his [[memory]].

verbs.wrong: To break the rock around a bone

chunks.text: About 61 percent of Gus is real bone, which is a lot for a T. rex. Most skeletons in museums are largely [[plaster]]. The [[skull]] is almost [[undamaged]]. Gus also kept its [[furcula]], a thin V shaped bone across the chest that we call the wishbone in a chicken. That bone is [[fragile]] and it very rarely {{shows up}} in a fossil this old. Those three things together are why the bidding {{shot up}}.

Scientists were less pleased than the sellers. The incoming president of a society of fossil experts said she hoped the buyer would {{hand over}} the skeleton to a museum. Once a fossil is {{locked away}} in a private house, researchers cannot [[measure]] it, and no public museum can {{keep up with}} private [[bidders]] at these prices. The buyer has not {{come forward}}. So the most complete Tyrannosaurus to reach the market in years now [[belongs to]] somebody nobody can name, and the people who wanted to study it have been {{shut out}}.
